options.rationale: Correct: weighs risk, impact, and recovery.

options.text: Deploy it to the servers immediately
options.rationale: Fast, but skips testing on critical systems.

options.text: Wait for the next annual maintenance cycle
options.rationale: Leaves a critical flaw open for months.

options.text: Skip it, since patching risks downtime
options.rationale: Leaves the risk unaddressed.

questions.explanation: Remediation considerations weigh risk and priority, business impact, testing, maintenance windows, dependencies, and a rollback plan. Test before wide deployment, and prioritize by risk.
questions.discriminator_tested: Test before wide deployment; prioritize by risk.

questions.stem: Before donating old PCs, a technician deletes the users' files and empties the Recycle Bin. What BEST describes the problem?

options.text: The PCs should be reformatted instead
options.rationale: A standard format also leaves data recoverable.

options.text: The donation wasn't documented
options.rationale: Documentation matters, but the data is the main problem.

options.text: Deleted data can still be recovered
options.rationale: Correct: deleting isn't sanitizing.

options.text: Recycle Bin contents are encrypted
options.rationale: They aren't.

questions.explanation: Destruction and disposal means retiring devices and media so data can't be recovered, following policy and documenting it. Deleting files isn't sanitizing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Deleting files is not sanitizing.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a low-level format from a standard format?

options.text: It rebuilds the file system tables
options.rationale: That is what a standard format does.

options.text: It takes much longer to complete
options.rationale: Usually true, but not the defining difference.

options.text: It overwrites the sectors themselves
options.rationale: Correct: a standard format only rebuilds file system structures.

options.text: It encrypts the drive before formatting
options.rationale: Formatting doesn't encrypt.

questions.explanation: A standard format rebuilds file system structures; a low-level format overwrites every sector. A standard format leaves data recoverable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard format leaves data recoverable.

questions.stem: Drives that held top-secret data are being retired and won't be reused. Which method BEST fits?

options.text: Deleting the files
options.rationale: Leaves data recoverable.

options.text: Physical destruction
options.rationale: Correct: the most certain method, and reuse isn't needed.

options.text: A standard format
options.rationale: Leaves data recoverable.

options.text: A multi-pass overwrite
options.rationale: Suits reuse, but the highest sensitivity points to destruction.

questions.explanation: Hard drive sanitization makes data unrecoverable; the method depends on data sensitivity and whether the drive will be reused. Reuse allows overwrite or wipe; the highest sensitivity points to destruction.
questions.discriminator_tested: Highest sensitivity points to destruction.

questions.stem: A team plans to overwrite retired SSDs with zeros before reselling them. What is the MAIN concern?

options.text: Zeros can be decrypted back to data
options.rationale: Overwriting isn't encryption.

options.text: SSDs may keep data in unreachable cells
options.rationale: Correct: wear levelling and spare cells can escape an overwrite.

options.text: Overwriting takes a long time
options.rationale: True, but time isn't the security concern.

options.text: Degaussing would be faster
options.rationale: Degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.

questions.explanation: Overwrite writes patterns over all addressable areas of the media in one or more passes. It allows reuse but is less reliable on SSDs and failed sectors.
questions.discriminator_tested: Overwrite is less reliable on SSDs.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes using a drive wipe tool from overwriting a drive by hand?

options.text: It physically destroys the drive
options.rationale: Wiping leaves the drive usable.

options.text: It supports reusing the drive
options.rationale: Both approaches allow reuse.

options.text: Automated, verified, and reportable
options.rationale: Correct: the tool erases the whole drive and documents it.

options.text: It leaves the data recoverable
options.rationale: A proper wipe makes data unrecoverable.

questions.explanation: A drive wipe is a tool-driven erase of the whole drive (wipe utilities, firmware secure erase, cryptographic erase), often with verification. It is automated and reportable, supports reuse, and typically applies overwrite.
questions.discriminator_tested: Drive wipe: automated and reportable.

questions.stem: Which two are physical destruction methods for drives? (Choose two.)

options.text: A seven-pass overwrite
options.rationale: An overwrite leaves the drive reusable.

options.text: A firmware secure erase
options.rationale: A wipe method; the drive survives.

options.text: Shredding the drive
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Deleting the partitions
options.rationale: Leaves data recoverable.

options.text: Degaussing a hard disk
options.rationale: Correct: it destroys magnetic media (not SSDs).

questions.explanation: Physical destruction means shredding, crushing, incineration, or degaussing (magnetic media). It is the most certain method and leaves the drive unusable; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Destruction is most certain; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.

questions.stem: Ransomware encrypted a file server and also the backup share mapped on that server, and restores now fail. What was the MAIN weakness?

options.text: The backups were too large
options.rationale: Size isn't why they failed.

options.text: Backups weren't tested regularly
options.rationale: A real gap, but even tested backups were reachable here.

options.text: No offline or offsite backup copy
options.rationale: Correct: the ransomware could reach every copy.

options.text: The antivirus definitions were old
options.rationale: Might explain the infection, not the failed recovery.

questions.explanation: Data backups are copies of data for recovery after loss, failure, or ransomware. An untested backup is unproven, and offline or offsite copies resist ransomware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Offline or offsite copies resist ransomware.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes regulatory compliance from internal security policy?

options.text: They are the same thing with different names
options.rationale: One is external, the other internal.

options.text: Compliance usually involves audits
options.rationale: True, but internal policies are audited too.

options.text: Compliance requirements are imposed from outside
options.rationale: Correct: laws and industry rules such as HIPAA and PCI DSS.

options.text: Policy is enforced by law; compliance is optional
options.rationale: This is reversed.

questions.explanation: Regulatory compliance means meeting external legal and industry requirements for handling data (for example HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). It is externally imposed, unlike internal policy.
questions.discriminator_tested: Compliance is externally imposed.

questions.stem: A company wants to fully wipe any lost phone remotely, with no staff privacy concerns. Which device model BEST fits?

options.text: BYOD phones with a screen-lock rule
options.rationale: A screen lock doesn't allow remote wiping.

options.text: Company-owned phones
options.rationale: Correct: full organizational control, no personal data at stake.

options.text: BYOD phones enrolled in MDM
options.rationale: Possible, but wiping personal phones raises privacy issues.

options.text: Personal phones with no enrollment
options.rationale: No control at all.

questions.explanation: BYOD means employee-owned devices; organization-owned devices are under full organizational control. Ownership drives how much control and privacy there is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ownership drives control and privacy.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by v2 fix1 (answer echoed the stem), 2026-10-21

questions.stem: A company needs to enroll 500 phones, push Wi-Fi and email settings to them, and remotely lock lost ones. What BEST fits?

options.text: A SIEM dashboard
options.rationale: A SIEM analyzes logs.

options.text: An asset tag on each phone
options.rationale: Tags identify devices; they don't manage them.

options.text: A captive portal
options.rationale: A portal gates network access; it doesn't manage phones.

options.text: An MDM platform
options.rationale: Correct: enroll, configure, and enforce policy centrally.

questions.explanation: MDM is a central platform to enroll, configure, and enforce policy on mobile devices, including remote lock and wipe. Configuration management, app distribution, and encryption are things it manages.
questions.discriminator_tested: MDM is the platform.

questions.stem: A management tool produces the report below. What BEST describes what it shows?
questions.exhibit:
Baseline: WIN11-STD v4 (approved 2026-09-01)
Host      Setting                     Baseline   Actual
LT-0112   SMBv1                       Disabled   Enabled
LT-0112   Firewall (Public profile)   On         Off
LT-0157   (no deviations)

options.text: LT-0112 has two settings changed
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't name what the report detects.

options.text: A failed patch deployment
options.rationale: Nothing here is about patches.

options.text: Malware detected on LT-0157
options.rationale: LT-0157 has no deviations at all.

options.text: Drift from the baseline
options.rationale: Correct: LT-0112 no longer matches the approved configuration.

questions.explanation: Configuration management maintains consistent, documented, approved configurations (baselines) under change control, which lets it detect configuration drift.
questions.discriminator_tested: Baseline plus change control detects drift.

questions.stem: Managed phones may install apps from a company-approved catalog and nowhere else. Which MDM capability does this describe?

options.text: Configuration baselines
options.rationale: Settings consistency, not app sources.

options.text: Remote wipe
options.rationale: Erases a lost device.

options.text: App distribution controls
options.rationale: Correct: governs software sources on managed devices.

options.text: Data encryption
options.rationale: Protects stored data, not app sources.

questions.explanation: App distribution controls which apps are installed and from where (a managed app store, allow and block lists). It governs software sources on managed devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: App distribution governs software sources.

questions.stem: A managed laptop has full-disk encryption. Which risk does this MOST directly reduce?

options.text: Data exposure if the laptop is lost
options.rationale: Correct: the disk is unreadable without the key.

options.text: Network eavesdropping on its traffic
options.rationale: Disk encryption doesn't touch network traffic.

options.text: Phishing emails reaching the user
options.rationale: Email filtering and training address that.

options.text: Malware infection while it is in use
options.rationale: While running, the disk is unlocked.

questions.explanation: Data encryption protects data on the device, for example with full-disk encryption. A lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by v2 fix1 (answer echoed the stem), 2026-10-21

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes endpoint recovery from endpoint protection?

options.text: Recovery runs antimalware scans continuously
options.rationale: Continuous scanning is protection.

options.text: Recovery restores; protection prevents
options.rationale: Correct: after a problem vs before it.

options.text: They are two names for EDR
options.rationale: EDR is one protection control.

options.text: Recovery uses backups or reimaging
options.rationale: True of recovery, but it doesn't contrast it with protection.

questions.explanation: Endpoint recovery restores an endpoint to a known-good state (restore from backup, reimage, rebuild) after a problem; endpoint protection tries to prevent the problem.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recovery after a problem; protection tries to prevent it.

questions.stem: Which two are endpoint protection controls? (Choose two.)

options.text: Nightly backups to tape
options.rationale: Supports recovery, not protection.

options.text: Host-based firewall
options.rationale: Correct: preventive control on the device.

options.text: A drive shredder
options.rationale: A disposal tool.

options.text: EDR agent on the laptop
options.rationale: Correct: detective and responsive control on the device.

options.text: An IP scanner on the subnet
options.rationale: A network discovery tool.

questions.explanation: Endpoint protection is the controls on the device itself: antimalware, host-based firewall, host intrusion detection, and EDR. They are preventive and detective controls on the endpoint.
questions.discriminator_tested: Preventive and detective controls on the endpoint itself.

questions.stem: What is the MAIN trade-off of cloud-based endpoint protection?

options.text: Signatures are updated quickly
options.rationale: The benefit, without the trade-off.

options.text: Fast updates, but it needs internet
options.rationale: Correct: fast and works off-network, but relies on connectivity.

options.text: It works on the office network alone
options.rationale: It covers devices off-network too.

options.text: It replaces the need for local agents
options.rationale: It still relies on an agent on each endpoint.

questions.explanation: Cloud-based protection delivers or analyzes endpoint security through the cloud (cloud signatures, threat intelligence, a central console). It gives fast updates and off-network coverage but needs connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: Fast updates and off-network coverage; needs connectivity.

questions.stem: An analyst reviews the scan history below for one laptop. What do these logs MOST importantly show?
questions.exhibit:
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-14 02:00  Completed  0 threats  Defs: 2026-07-30
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-15 02:00  Failed     service stopped
Scheduled scan  LT-0201  2026-10-16 02:00  Failed     service stopped

options.text: Failed scans, stale definitions
options.rationale: Correct: scans aren't running, and definitions are months old.

options.text: Scans are running too often
options.rationale: They are failing, not too frequent.

options.text: The laptop is free of malware
options.rationale: A clean log doesn't prove safety.

options.text: No threats were found on 14 October
options.rationale: True, but meaningless with outdated definitions.

questions.explanation: Reviewing scan logs means examining antimalware and vulnerability scan results for detections, failures, and patterns. A clean log doesn't prove safety; check that scans ran and definitions were current.
questions.discriminator_tested: A clean log doesn't prove safety.

questions.stem: Which sequence matches the malware remediation process?

options.text: Identify, quarantine, disable Restore, remediate, update, enable Restore, educate
options.rationale: Correct: the seven steps in order.

options.text: Quarantine, identify, remediate, disable Restore, update, enable Restore, educate
options.rationale: Symptoms are confirmed first, and Restore is disabled before cleaning.

options.text: Identify, quarantine, remediate, disable Restore, enable Restore, update, educate
options.rationale: Restore must be off before cleaning, and updates come before re-enabling it.

options.text: Identify, remediate, quarantine, educate, disable Restore, update, enable Restore
options.rationale: Quarantine must come before cleaning.

questions.explanation: The malware remediation process has seven ordered steps: identify and verify symptoms; quarantine; disable System Restore; remediate; schedule scans and run updates; re-enable System Restore and create restore points; educate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Sequence matters.

questions.stem: A user reports pop-ups, a changed browser home page, and antivirus that won't start. Following the malware remediation process, what is the FIRST step?

options.text: Verify it's malware
options.rationale: Correct: confirm the symptoms before acting.

options.text: Disconnect the PC from the network
options.rationale: Quarantine is the second step.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan
options.rationale: Scanning is part of remediation, step four.

options.text: Reinstall the operating system
options.rationale: Premature, and not the first step.

questions.explanation: Identifying and verifying malware symptoms means gathering the signs (slowness, pop-ups, redirects, disabled antivirus, unknown processes) and confirming malware. It is the first step: confirm before acting.
questions.discriminator_tested: First step: confirm before acting.

questions.stem: A PC is confirmed infected with a worm. Per the malware remediation process, what should the technician do NEXT?

options.text: Teach the user about phishing
options.rationale: Education is the last step.

options.text: Scan it with updated antimalware
options.rationale: Cleaning comes after quarantine and disabling Restore.

options.text: Disable System Restore
options.rationale: That is the step after quarantine.

options.text: Isolate it from the network
options.rationale: Correct: quarantine stops the spread before cleaning.

questions.explanation: Quarantining an infected system means isolating it from the network (disconnecting it or moving it to an isolated VLAN). It stops the spread before cleaning.
questions.discriminator_tested: Quarantine stops spread before cleaning.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why System Restore is turned off before cleaning an infected Windows PC?

options.text: Restore points may hold copies of the malware
options.rationale: Correct: they could reintroduce it later.

options.text: It stops the malware spreading on the network
options.rationale: Quarantine does that.

options.text: It is a required step in the process
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: It frees disk space for the scan
options.rationale: Space isn't the reason.

questions.explanation: Disabling System Restore before cleaning keeps malware in old restore points from being preserved, because restore points can hold malware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Restore points can hold malware.

questions.stem: A rootkit hides from the antivirus while Windows is running. Which approach BEST removes it?

options.text: Scan from rescue media outside Windows
options.rationale: Correct: the rootkit can't hide when its OS isn't running.

options.text: Disable UAC and rescan
options.rationale: UAC has nothing to do with detection.

options.text: Update definitions and rescan normally
options.rationale: Necessary, but the rootkit still hides from a scan run inside Windows.

options.text: Delete the System32 folder
options.rationale: That destroys Windows.

questions.explanation: Remediating infected systems means updating antimalware, scanning, and removing the malware, using safe mode or rescue media when needed. Use current definitions; rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by v2 fix1 (answer echoed the stem), 2026-10-21

questions.stem: Malware got in through an unpatched browser plug-in and has now been removed. What BEST explains why the process still requires patching and scheduled scans?

options.text: To re-enable System Restore
options.rationale: That is the next step, not this one's purpose.

options.text: To restore the files the malware deleted
options.rationale: Patches don't restore files.

options.text: To close the hole that let it in
options.rationale: Correct: otherwise the same flaw lets it straight back in.

options.text: To keep the antivirus definitions current
options.rationale: Part of it, but patching the entry point matters most.

questions.explanation: Scheduling scans and running updates means patching the OS and applications, updating signatures, and scheduling recurring scans. It closes the hole that let the malware in.
questions.discriminator_tested: Closes the hole that let the malware in.

questions.stem: When should System Restore be turned back on and a new restore point created?

options.text: After the system is verified clean
options.rationale: Correct: so the restore point captures a clean state.

options.text: Before running the malware scan
options.rationale: A restore point then would capture the malware.

options.text: It stays off on a previously infected PC
options.rationale: It should be re-enabled once the PC is clean.

options.text: Right after quarantining the PC
options.rationale: The PC is still infected then.

questions.explanation: Turn System Restore back on and create a fresh restore point only after the system is verified clean.
questions.discriminator_tested: Only after the system is verified clean.

questions.stem: A user's PC was cleaned of malware that arrived in a phishing email. A week later it is reinfected the same way. Which step was MOST likely skipped?

options.text: Disabling System Restore
options.rationale: That affects cleanup, not how the user got phished again.

options.text: Quarantining the PC
options.rationale: Quarantine contains spread during cleaning.

options.text: Educating the user
options.rationale: Correct: the final step prevents a repeat.

options.text: Scheduling scans and updates
options.rationale: Scans can't stop a user clicking a link.

questions.explanation: Educating end users (phishing, safe downloads, reporting) is the final step of the malware remediation process, and it prevents recurrence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Education is the final step; prevents recurrence.
questions.retired_reason: Superseded by v2 fix1 (answer echoed the stem), 2026-10-21

questions.stem: A technician wants to see which ports a Windows server is listening on right now, from the server itself, without scanning it over the network. Which command BEST fits?

options.text: tracert localhost
options.rationale: Shows a path, not ports.

options.text: netstat -an
options.rationale: Correct: a local view of listening ports and connections.

options.text: nmap localhost
options.rationale: A scan, which is what the technician wants to avoid.

options.text: nslookup localhost
options.rationale: Resolves a name.

questions.explanation: netstat shows active connections, listening ports, routing table, and interface statistics on the local host (netstat -an). It is a local view; nmap probes hosts over the network.
questions.discriminator_tested: netstat: local view of what is connected or listening.

questions.stem: A technician runs the command below. What does the output BEST show?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> nslookup intranet.corp.example.com
Server:   dns1.corp.example.com
Address:  10.1.9.53

*** dns1.corp.example.com can't find intranet.corp.example.com: Non-existent domain

options.text: The intranet web server is down
options.rationale: DNS says nothing about the web server's state.

options.text: The PC has no route to its DNS server
options.rationale: dns1 replied, so the PC reached it.

options.text: The DNS server has no record for that name
options.rationale: Correct: the server answered, saying the name doesn't exist.

options.text: The lookup for the intranet failed
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

questions.explanation: nslookup queries DNS to resolve names to IPs and back. It is the basic DNS troubleshooting tool on Windows and Linux; 'Non-existent domain' means the server answered that the name isn't in DNS.
questions.discriminator_tested: nslookup: basic DNS troubleshooting.

questions.stem: Compared with nslookup, what BEST describes the extra value of dig?

options.text: It traces each router hop to the server
options.rationale: That is traceroute.

options.text: Record sections, TTLs, and query time
options.rationale: Correct: much more detail about the answer.

options.text: It captures DNS packets on the wire
options.rationale: That is tcpdump.

options.text: It runs on Linux and macOS
options.rationale: True, but platform isn't added value.

questions.explanation: dig is a detailed DNS query tool (dig example.com MX). It is more detailed than nslookup, showing record sections, TTL, and query time.
questions.discriminator_tested: dig is more detailed than nslookup.

questions.stem: A technician runs the tests below. Which conclusion is BEST supported?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> ping 10.1.9.15
Reply from 10.1.9.15: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128
Reply from 10.1.9.15: bytes=32 time=1ms TTL=128

C:\> ping 10.1.9.16
Request timed out.
Request timed out.

options.text: 10.1.9.15 is reachable from this PC
options.rationale: True, but it says nothing about .16.

options.text: .15 answers; .16 is down or filtering ICMP
options.rationale: Correct: silence from .16 has more than one cause.

options.text: Both hosts are blocking ICMP
options.rationale: .15 replied to ICMP.

options.text: 10.1.9.16 is definitely powered off
options.rationale: A failed ping doesn't prove the host is down.

questions.explanation: ping tests reachability and round-trip time with ICMP echo. A failed ping doesn't prove the host is down, because ICMP may be blocked.
questions.discriminator_tested: A failed ping does not prove the host is down.

questions.stem: What does tracert reveal that ping doesn't?

options.text: Whether the destination is reachable
options.rationale: ping already shows that.

options.text: Where on the path it fails
options.rationale: Correct: it lists each hop up to the failure.

options.text: Which ports are open on each router
options.rationale: That needs a port scanner.

options.text: Round-trip time to the destination
options.rationale: ping already shows that.

questions.explanation: tracert (Windows) or traceroute (Linux/macOS) shows each hop along the path to a destination. It locates where along the path connectivity fails.
questions.discriminator_tested: tracert locates where along the path connectivity fails.

questions.stem: Which two tasks need a packet capture tool such as tcpdump rather than netstat? (Choose two.)

options.text: Showing established connections and their PIDs
options.rationale: netstat -ano does that.

options.text: Seeing each packet of a TCP handshake
options.rationale: Correct: needs the actual packets.

options.text: Listing the host's listening ports
options.rationale: netstat does that.

options.text: Testing reachability with ICMP echo
options.rationale: That is ping.

options.text: Reading the contents of DNS queries
options.rationale: Correct: needs the actual packets.

questions.explanation: tcpdump is command-line packet capture and analysis. It captures actual packets; netstat only lists connections.
questions.discriminator_tested: tcpdump captures packets; netstat lists connections.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes nmap from netstat?

options.text: nmap can detect service versions
options.rationale: True, but not the fundamental difference.

options.text: netstat probes other hosts; nmap reports the local one
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: nmap probes other hosts; netstat, the local one
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: nmap captures packet contents
options.rationale: That is tcpdump.

questions.explanation: nmap scans hosts for live devices, open ports, services, and OS details; it probes other hosts. netstat reports on the local host.
questions.discriminator_tested: nmap probes other hosts; netstat reports the local host.

questions.stem: A screen-lock setting isn't taking effect on a PC. The output below is from that PC. What BEST explains why?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> gpresult /r
COMPUTER SETTINGS
    Applied Group Policy Objects
        Default Domain Policy
        Workstation Baseline
    The following GPOs were not applied because they were filtered out
        Screen Lock Policy
            Filtering:  Denied (Security)

options.text: Security filtering denied it
options.rationale: Correct: the GPO was filtered out by its security filtering.

options.text: The Default Domain Policy overrides it
options.rationale: The output shows filtering, not an override.

options.text: The PC has lost contact with the domain
options.rationale: Other GPOs applied, so it reached the domain.

options.text: The Screen Lock Policy wasn't applied
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

questions.explanation: gpresult shows the Group Policy settings applied to a user or computer (gpresult /r). It is Windows-only and confirms which policies actually applied, and why others didn't.
questions.discriminator_tested: gpresult confirms which policies actually applied.

questions.stem: A port scan of a server returns the lines below. What does 'filtered' on port 443 MOST likely mean?
questions.exhibit:
PORT      STATE     SERVICE
22/tcp    open      ssh
80/tcp    closed    http
443/tcp   filtered  https

options.text: The scanner got no clear answer from 443
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say the likely reason.

options.text: A firewall likely dropped the probe
options.rationale: Correct: no answer came back, typical of a firewall.

options.text: HTTPS is listening and accepting connections
options.rationale: That would show as open.

options.text: The host refused the connection with a reset
options.rationale: That would show as closed.

questions.explanation: A port scanner probes a host to find open, closed, or filtered ports. Filtered means the probe got no clear answer, usually because a firewall dropped it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Port scanner reports open, closed, or filtered.

questions.stem: A security team runs iPerf against a server, expecting it to list the server's open ports. What is the MAIN problem?

options.text: iPerf scans one port at a time
options.rationale: iPerf doesn't scan ports at all.

options.text: iPerf supports UDP alone
options.rationale: iPerf tests TCP and UDP.

options.text: iPerf needs a server running at the far end
options.rationale: True, but even then it wouldn't list ports.

options.text: iPerf measures throughput, not open ports
options.rationale: Correct: it's a performance tool.

questions.explanation: iPerf measures network throughput between two endpoints (client and server, TCP or UDP). It is performance testing, not security scanning.
questions.discriminator_tested: iPerf is performance testing, not security scanning.

questions.stem: A ping sweep of a user subnet returns the results below. What is the BEST next step for 10.1.4.88?
questions.exhibit:
IP scan 10.1.4.0/24 (ping sweep)
10.1.4.1    00:1a:2b:3c:4d:01   Cisco Systems      (gateway, in inventory)
10.1.4.20   3c:52:82:aa:10:7e   Dell               (LT-0112, in inventory)
10.1.4.88   b8:27:eb:5f:22:91   Raspberry Pi Fdn   (not in inventory)

options.text: Investigate it as a rogue
options.rationale: Correct: an unknown device on a user subnet needs checking.

options.text: Ignore it, since it answered the ping
options.rationale: Answering a ping doesn't make it authorized.

options.text: Run iPerf against it to test its speed
options.rationale: Throughput isn't the question.

options.text: Add it to the hardware inventory
options.rationale: Premature: first find out what it is and whether it belongs.

questions.explanation: An IP scanner discovers active devices across an address range (a ping sweep). It answers 'which hosts are on this network?' and finds rogue devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: IP scanner finds rogue devices.

questions.stem: Which two fields belong in a hardware inventory record? (Choose two.)

options.text: User's password hint
options.rationale: Never belongs in an inventory.

options.text: Serial number
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Assigned owner and location
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Open TCP ports
options.rationale: A scan result, not an inventory field.

options.text: Installed software versions
options.rationale: That belongs in the software inventory.

questions.explanation: A hardware inventory records physical devices: type, serial, owner, location, and status. You can't protect devices you don't know exist.
questions.discriminator_tested: Hardware inventory: type, serial, owner, location, status.

questions.stem: IT needs one place to track each laptop from purchase, through assignment and repairs, to secure disposal. What BEST fits?

options.text: A software inventory
options.rationale: Tracks installed software, not device lifecycles.

options.text: An asset management system
options.rationale: Correct: the system of record for the whole lifecycle.

options.text: Asset tags alone
options.rationale: Tags identify devices but hold no history.

options.text: A SIEM platform
options.rationale: A SIEM analyzes logs.

questions.explanation: Asset management systems track assets from purchase through disposal; they are the system of record. A tag is only the physical identifier.
questions.discriminator_tested: Asset management system = system of record.

questions.stem: Which statement about asset tags is BEST?

options.text: They store the device's full history
options.rationale: The asset management system holds the history.

options.text: They encrypt the device's storage
options.rationale: Tags are labels.

options.text: They carry a unique ID, often as a barcode
options.rationale: True, but the purpose is linking the device to its record.

options.text: They link device to record
options.rationale: Correct: they tie the physical device to its inventory record.

questions.explanation: An asset tag is a physical, barcode, or RFID label with a unique ID on a device. It ties the physical device to its inventory record.
questions.discriminator_tested: Asset tag ties the device to its record.

questions.stem: Which two problems can a software inventory reveal? (Choose two.)

options.text: Failing hard drives
options.rationale: A hardware health issue.

options.text: Unknown devices plugged into the network
options.rationale: An IP scan or hardware inventory finds those.

options.text: Unlicensed or unauthorized programs
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Vulnerable versions of installed apps
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: Weak Wi-Fi encryption
options.rationale: A network configuration issue.

questions.explanation: A software inventory records installed software, versions, and licenses. Versions reveal vulnerable software, and the inventory also flags unauthorized or unlicensed programs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Versions reveal vulnerable software; flags unlicensed programs.

questions.stem: Which two actions are remediation? (Choose two.)

options.text: Isolating a device that can't be fixed
options.rationale: Correct: mitigates the finding.

options.text: Patching a vulnerable server
options.rationale: Correct: fixes the finding.

options.text: Filing the scan report
options.rationale: Filing fixes nothing.

options.text: Running a vulnerability scan weekly
options.rationale: That is discovery.

options.text: Buying a second scanner
options.rationale: More discovery, no fixes.

questions.explanation: Remediation means fixing or mitigating identified vulnerabilities and non-compliance: patch, reconfigure, remove, or isolate. Discovery alone fixes nothing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Remediation acts on findings.

questions.stem: A patch broke a payroll application, and IT couldn't undo it for two days. Which remediation consideration was MOST clearly missing?

options.text: Testing before wide deployment
options.rationale: Also important, but the two days of no undo point to rollback.

options.text: A tested rollback plan
options.rationale: Correct: the inability to undo is the failure described.

options.text: A faster internet connection
options.rationale: Irrelevant.

options.text: A larger maintenance window
options.rationale: More time wouldn't have given a way back.

questions.explanation: Remediation considerations weigh risk and priority, business impact, testing, maintenance windows, dependencies, and a rollback plan.
questions.discriminator_tested: Keep a rollback plan.

questions.stem: Policy requires proof that every retired drive was sanitized. What should the disposal process BEST include to satisfy this?

options.text: Deleting the files on each drive
options.rationale: Deleting isn't sanitizing.

options.text: A verbal sign-off from the technician
options.rationale: Not verifiable later.

options.text: Sanitizing each drive before it leaves
options.rationale: Necessary, but without a record there's no proof.

options.text: Sanitization records per drive
options.rationale: Correct: documentation is the proof.

questions.explanation: Destruction and disposal means retiring devices and media so data can't be recovered, following policy and documenting it. Deleting files isn't sanitizing.
questions.discriminator_tested: Follow policy and document it.

questions.stem: A drive is given a quick standard format before being resold. What can a buyer MOST likely do?

options.text: Nothing; the format erased the data
options.rationale: A standard format rebuilds structures; the data remains.

options.text: Use the drive normally
options.rationale: True, but it misses the risk.

options.text: Recover much of the old data
options.rationale: Correct: a standard format leaves the data in place.

options.text: Read the file names alone
options.rationale: Contents are often recoverable too.

questions.explanation: A standard format rebuilds file system structures; a low-level format overwrites every sector. A standard format leaves data recoverable.
questions.discriminator_tested: Standard format leaves data recoverable.

questions.stem: Hard drives from a call center will be reused internally. Which method BEST balances security and reuse?

options.text: Degaussing them
options.rationale: Destroys the drives, preventing reuse.

options.text: Shredding them
options.rationale: Destroys the drives.

options.text: A standard format, then reuse
options.rationale: Leaves data recoverable.

options.text: A verified drive wipe
options.rationale: Correct: unrecoverable data, and the drives stay usable.

questions.explanation: Hard drive sanitization makes data unrecoverable; the method depends on sensitivity and whether the drive will be reused. Reuse allows overwrite or wipe.
questions.discriminator_tested: Reuse allows overwrite or wipe.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why an overwrite is usually fine for a working hard disk but questionable for an SSD?

options.text: SSDs store data differently from HDDs
options.rationale: True, but vague; it doesn't say what defeats the overwrite.

options.text: SSDs are faster to overwrite
options.rationale: Speed isn't the issue.

options.text: SSDs remap cells the overwrite may not reach
options.rationale: Correct: wear levelling leaves data in cells outside the addressable space.

options.text: HDDs encrypt data automatically
options.rationale: They don't.

questions.explanation: Overwrite writes patterns over all addressable areas in one or more passes. It allows reuse but is less reliable on SSDs and failed sectors.
questions.discriminator_tested: Overwrite is less reliable on SSDs.

questions.stem: A company will redeploy 200 laptops with SSDs and must prove that each was erased. Which method BEST fits?

options.text: A quick format on each laptop's drive
options.rationale: Leaves data recoverable.

options.text: A drive wipe with firmware secure erase and a report
options.rationale: Correct: reliable on SSDs, reusable, and documented.

options.text: Degaussing each SSD before reissue
options.rationale: Degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.

options.text: A multi-pass overwrite of each drive's sectors
options.rationale: Allows reuse, but overwriting is less reliable on SSDs.

questions.explanation: A drive wipe is a tool-driven erase of the whole drive (wipe utilities, firmware secure erase, cryptographic erase), often with verification. It is automated and reportable and supports reuse.
questions.discriminator_tested: Drive wipe: automated, reportable, supports reuse.

questions.stem: A defense contractor plans to degauss its failed SSDs before disposal. Which answer is BEST?

options.text: Degaussing takes too long for large batches
options.rationale: Time isn't the problem; it doesn't work at all.

options.text: The SSDs must be documented first
options.rationale: Documenting is good practice, but the method itself fails.

options.text: It doesn't work on SSDs; shred them
options.rationale: Correct: SSDs aren't magnetic media.

options.text: Degaussing leaves SSDs reusable
options.rationale: Degaussing, where it works, destroys drives.

questions.explanation: Physical destruction means shredding, crushing, incineration, or degaussing (magnetic media). It is the most certain method and leaves the drive unusable; degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.
questions.discriminator_tested: Degaussing doesn't work on SSDs.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why an untested backup is described as 'unproven'?

options.text: It is stored without encryption at rest
options.rationale: Encryption is a separate concern.

options.text: It might be stored at another site
options.rationale: Offsite storage is good practice.

options.text: No one knows it can actually be restored
options.rationale: Correct: only a restore test proves a backup works.

options.text: It may be older than the last change
options.rationale: Possibly, but even a current backup is unproven until restored.

questions.explanation: Data backups are copies of data for recovery after loss, failure, or ransomware. An untested backup is unproven, and offline or offsite copies resist ransomware.
questions.discriminator_tested: An untested backup is unproven.

questions.stem: Which two are examples of regulatory compliance requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: An internal acceptable use policy
options.rationale: Internal policy.

options.text: HIPAA rules for patient health information
options.rationale: Correct: an external legal requirement.

options.text: The company's own password policy
options.rationale: Internal policy.

options.text: A vendor's recommended configuration baseline
options.rationale: A recommendation, not a legal or industry mandate.

options.text: PCI DSS rules for handling card data
options.rationale: Correct: an external industry requirement.

questions.explanation: Regulatory compliance means meeting external legal and industry requirements for handling data (for example HIPAA, PCI DSS, GDPR). It is externally imposed, unlike internal policy.
questions.discriminator_tested: Compliance is externally imposed.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why BYOD gives a company less control than organization-owned devices?

options.text: BYOD devices come in many makes and models
options.rationale: True and a challenge, but ownership is the root of it.

options.text: BYOD devices are barred from MDM enrollment
options.rationale: BYOD devices can be enrolled.

options.text: Company-owned devices tend to be newer
options.rationale: Age doesn't decide control.

options.text: The employee owns the device and its personal data
options.rationale: Correct: ownership limits control and raises privacy concerns.

questions.explanation: BYOD means employee-owned devices; organization-owned devices are under full organizational control. Ownership drives how much control and privacy there is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ownership drives control and privacy.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes how MDM relates to configuration management, app distribution, and data encryption on mobile devices?

options.text: They are separate products that replace MDM
options.rationale: They are features delivered through MDM.

options.text: MDM handles encryption and nothing else
options.rationale: It covers far more.

options.text: MDM is another name for configuration management
options.rationale: Configuration management is one thing MDM does.

options.text: MDM is the platform that manages those three
options.rationale: Correct: they are capabilities it enforces.

questions.explanation: MDM is a central platform to enroll, configure, and enforce policy on mobile devices (remote lock and wipe). Configuration management, app distribution, and data encryption are things it manages.
questions.discriminator_tested: MDM is the platform; the others are what it manages.

questions.stem: Admins change server settings directly whenever they like, with no record, and the servers slowly diverge from one another. What is MOST clearly missing?

options.text: An approved baseline under change control
options.rationale: Correct: it keeps configurations consistent and drift visible.

options.text: A faster patch deployment process
options.rationale: Patching speed isn't the issue.

options.text: Documentation of each change
options.rationale: Part of it, but without a baseline there's nothing to compare against.

options.text: More powerful server hardware
options.rationale: Irrelevant to configuration drift.

questions.explanation: Configuration management maintains consistent, documented, approved configurations (baselines) under change control, which detects configuration drift.
questions.discriminator_tested: Baseline plus change control detects drift.

questions.stem: Staff phones keep installing a malicious flashlight app from a third-party store. Which MDM control BEST stops this?

options.text: An app allow list from a managed app store
options.rationale: Correct: governs where apps may come from.

options.text: Remote wipe of infected phones
options.rationale: Cleans up afterwards, but doesn't stop the installs.

options.text: Encrypting the storage on each phone
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't control app sources.

options.text: Requiring a stronger Wi-Fi passphrase
options.rationale: Unrelated to app installs.

questions.explanation: App distribution controls which apps are installed and from where (a managed app store, allow and block lists). It governs software sources on managed devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: App distribution governs software sources.

questions.stem: A laptop with a fully encrypted drive is stolen from a car while powered off. What is the MOST likely outcome for its data?

options.text: The thief can read it by moving the drive
options.rationale: Moving an encrypted drive doesn't decrypt it.

options.text: It stays unreadable to the thief without the key
options.rationale: Correct: the disk can't be read without the key.

options.text: The device can be wiped remotely
options.rationale: That is MDM, and the laptop may never come online.

options.text: It is protected while the laptop is powered off
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say what the thief can do.

questions.explanation: Data encryption protects data on the device, for example with full-disk encryption. A lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.
questions.discriminator_tested: A lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.

questions.stem: A PC is badly infected, and the business needs it back today with high confidence that it is clean. What is the BEST recovery approach?

options.text: Reimage it from a known-good image and restore data
options.rationale: Correct: returns it to a known-good state.

options.text: Run several antimalware scans until clean
options.rationale: Might work, but can't give the same confidence.

options.text: Use a System Restore point from last week
options.rationale: Restore points can contain malware.

options.text: Reboot it into safe mode and keep using it
options.rationale: Safe mode doesn't remove anything.

questions.explanation: Endpoint recovery restores an endpoint to a known-good state (restore from backup, reimage, rebuild); it is recovery after a problem, while protection tries to prevent it.
questions.discriminator_tested: Recovery restores a known-good state.

questions.stem: An EDR agent watches process behavior on each laptop and can kill suspicious processes. Which threat does it BEST address?

options.text: Lost laptops exposing their data
options.rationale: Encryption addresses that.

options.text: Malware running on the endpoint itself
options.rationale: Correct: detective and responsive control on the device.

options.text: Rogue devices joining the corporate network
options.rationale: NAC and IP scanning address that.

options.text: A failed hard drive losing data
options.rationale: Backups address that.

questions.explanation: Endpoint protection is the controls on the device itself: antimalware, host-based firewall, host intrusion detection, and EDR. They are preventive and detective controls on the endpoint.
questions.discriminator_tested: Endpoint protection = controls on the device itself.

questions.stem: A salesperson's laptop hasn't connected to the office network in two months. What BEST explains why cloud-based endpoint protection suits it?

options.text: It scans when the laptop is on the office LAN
options.rationale: The laptop is never on the LAN.

options.text: It works without any internet connection
options.rationale: It needs connectivity.

options.text: It updates and reports over the internet, from anywhere
options.rationale: Correct: off-network coverage.

options.text: It uses threat intelligence from many customers
options.rationale: A real benefit, but not why it suits an off-network laptop.

questions.explanation: Cloud-based protection delivers or analyzes endpoint security through the cloud (cloud signatures, threat intelligence, a central console). It gives fast updates and off-network coverage but needs connectivity.
questions.discriminator_tested: Off-network coverage; needs connectivity.

questions.stem: An antivirus console has shown 'No threats detected' for a server for a month. What should an analyst MOST importantly check before trusting that?

options.text: That the server's disk is encrypted
options.rationale: Encryption doesn't validate scan results.

options.text: That the firewall logs agree
options.rationale: Firewall logs don't confirm scan health.

options.text: That the server is still powered on and online
options.rationale: Worth knowing, but scan health is the key check.

options.text: That scans ran and definitions were current
options.rationale: Correct: a clean result means little otherwise.

questions.explanation: Reviewing scan logs means examining antimalware and vulnerability scan results for detections, failures, and patterns. A clean log doesn't prove safety; check that scans ran and definitions were current.
questions.discriminator_tested: Check that scans ran and definitions were current.

questions.stem: In the malware remediation process, which step comes immediately after disabling System Restore?

options.text: Educate the user about safe habits
options.rationale: That is the last step.

options.text: Remediate: update antimalware, scan, and remove
options.rationale: Correct: step four.

options.text: Quarantine the system from the network
options.rationale: That is step two.

options.text: Re-enable Restore and create a point
options.rationale: That is step six.

questions.explanation: The malware remediation process has seven ordered steps: identify and verify symptoms; quarantine; disable System Restore; remediate; schedule scans and run updates; re-enable System Restore and create restore points; educate users.
questions.discriminator_tested: Sequence matters.

questions.stem: Which two are common symptoms that suggest a malware infection? (Choose two.)

options.text: A new monitor not being detected
options.rationale: A hardware or driver issue.

options.text: A slow login caused by a busy DC
options.rationale: A server load issue.

options.text: Browser searches redirected to odd sites
options.rationale: Correct: a classic sign.

options.text: A backup job that failed because the disk was full
options.rationale: An ordinary capacity problem.

options.text: Antivirus that is disabled and won't restart
options.rationale: Correct: malware often disables protection.

questions.explanation: Identifying and verifying malware symptoms means gathering signs (slowness, pop-ups, redirects, disabled antivirus, unknown processes) and confirming malware. It is the first step: confirm before acting.
questions.discriminator_tested: Confirm symptoms before acting.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why quarantine comes before cleaning an infected PC?

options.text: It removes the malware from memory
options.rationale: Isolation doesn't remove anything.

options.text: It stops the spread while you clean it
options.rationale: Correct: isolation first.

options.text: It is the second step in the process
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: It restores the PC from a clean backup
options.rationale: That is recovery.

questions.explanation: Quarantining infected systems means isolating them from the network (disconnecting or moving them to an isolated VLAN). It stops the spread before cleaning.
questions.discriminator_tested: Quarantine stops spread before cleaning.

questions.stem: A technician cleans malware but forgot to disable System Restore first. Later, a user rolls the PC back to last week's restore point. What is the MOST likely result?

options.text: The PC goes back to last week's state
options.rationale: True, but it misses that last week's state includes the malware.

options.text: The malware returns from the old restore point
options.rationale: Correct: the restore point preserved it.

options.text: The malware is removed a second time
options.rationale: Nothing removes it; it comes back.

options.text: The restore fails, since scanning deleted it
options.rationale: Restore points survive scans.

questions.explanation: Disable System Restore before cleaning so malware in old restore points isn't preserved; restore points can hold malware.
questions.discriminator_tested: Restore points can hold malware.

questions.stem: Before scanning an infected PC, the technician updates the antimalware definitions. What BEST explains why?

options.text: Updates are part of the remediation step
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why.

options.text: Updating disables System Restore automatically
options.rationale: It doesn't.

options.text: Old definitions may not recognize this malware
options.rationale: Correct: use current definitions.

options.text: Updates quarantine the PC automatically
options.rationale: They don't.

questions.explanation: Remediating infected systems means updating antimalware, scanning, and removing the malware, using safe mode or rescue media when needed. Use current definitions.
questions.discriminator_tested: Use current definitions.

questions.stem: Which action belongs to the 'schedule scans and run updates' step of malware remediation?

options.text: Creating a fresh restore point
options.rationale: That is the next step.

options.text: Patching apps and the OS; scheduling scans
options.rationale: Correct: closes the hole and keeps checking.

options.text: Training the user to spot phishing
options.rationale: That is the final step.

options.text: Disconnecting the PC from the network
options.rationale: That is quarantine.

questions.explanation: Scheduling scans and running updates means patching the OS and applications, updating signatures, and scheduling recurring scans. It closes the hole that let the malware in.
questions.discriminator_tested: Closes the hole that let the malware in.

questions.stem: After cleaning, a technician re-enabled System Restore and created a restore point before verifying the PC was clean. The malware later came back from that point. What BEST describes what went wrong?

options.text: It was turned on before the PC was clean
options.rationale: Correct: the new restore point captured the malware.

options.text: The user wasn't educated
options.rationale: Education doesn't affect restore points.

options.text: A restore point was created
options.rationale: Creating one is correct; the timing was wrong.

options.text: System Restore stayed off too long
options.rationale: The problem was turning it on too early.

questions.explanation: Turn System Restore back on and create a fresh restore point only after the system is verified clean.
questions.discriminator_tested: Only after the system is verified clean.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why user education is the final step of malware remediation?

options.text: It re-enables System Restore
options.rationale: That is the step before.

options.text: It prevents the same infection from recurring
options.rationale: Correct.

options.text: It restores the user's deleted files
options.rationale: Training restores nothing.

options.text: It is the last item in the procedure
options.rationale: True, but that restates the question.

questions.explanation: Educating end users on phishing, safe downloads, and reporting is the final step of the malware remediation process, and it prevents recurrence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Education prevents recurrence.

questions.stem: A company wants to fully wipe any lost phone remotely, with no staff privacy concerns. Which device model BEST fits?

options.text: BYOD phones enrolled in MDM
options.rationale: Possible, but wiping personal phones raises privacy issues.

options.text: Organization-owned devices
options.rationale: Correct: full organizational control, no personal data at stake.

options.text: Personal phones with no enrollment
options.rationale: No control at all.

options.text: BYOD phones with a screen-lock rule
options.rationale: A screen lock doesn't allow remote wiping.

questions.explanation: BYOD means employee-owned devices; organization-owned devices are under full organizational control. Ownership drives how much control and privacy there is.
questions.discriminator_tested: Ownership drives control and privacy.

questions.stem: A managed laptop has full-disk encryption. Which risk does this MOST directly reduce?

options.text: Network eavesdropping on its traffic
options.rationale: Disk encryption doesn't touch network traffic.

options.text: Data exposure if the device is lost
options.rationale: Correct: the disk is unreadable without the key.

options.text: Phishing emails reaching the user
options.rationale: Email filtering and training address that.

options.text: Malware infection while it is in use
options.rationale: While running, the disk is unlocked.

questions.explanation: Data encryption protects data on the device, for example with full-disk encryption. A lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.
questions.discriminator_tested: Lost or stolen device doesn't expose readable data.

questions.stem: A rootkit hides from the antivirus while Windows is running. Which approach BEST removes it?

options.text: Disable UAC and rescan
options.rationale: UAC has nothing to do with detection.

options.text: Delete the System32 folder
options.rationale: That destroys Windows.

options.text: Update definitions and rescan normally
options.rationale: Necessary, but the rootkit still hides from a scan run inside Windows.

options.text: Scan from bootable rescue media
options.rationale: Correct: the rootkit can't hide when its OS isn't running.

questions.explanation: Remediating infected systems means updating antimalware, scanning, and removing the malware, using safe mode or rescue media when needed. Use current definitions; rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.
questions.discriminator_tested: Rescue media helps with stealthy malware such as rootkits.

questions.stem: A user's PC was cleaned of malware that arrived in a phishing email. A week later it is reinfected the same way. Which step was MOST likely skipped?

options.text: Security awareness training
options.rationale: Correct: the final step prevents a repeat.

options.text: Quarantining the PC
options.rationale: Quarantine contains spread during cleaning.

options.text: Disabling System Restore
options.rationale: That affects cleanup, not how the user got phished again.

options.text: Scheduling scans and updates
options.rationale: Scans can't stop a user clicking a link.

questions.explanation: Educating end users (phishing, safe downloads, reporting) is the final step of the malware remediation process, and it prevents recurrence.
questions.discriminator_tested: Education is the final step; prevents recurrence.
